Learning Objectives

Faculty emphasis rule from the handout
The handout states that blue-font concepts are important, bold material is high-yield, and the narrative under the slides is intentional study content. This companion therefore treats the narrative as examinable when it supports an objective.
LO 1. Describe basic human-cell ultrastructure, identify the major organelles and cytoplasmic components, and connect each organelle to its chief function.
LO 2. Explain plasma-membrane lipid asymmetry, how it is generated and maintained, and why disruption matters.

Current handout page 2. The four objectives define the lecture. The remainder of this companion is organized around them.
01Cell architecture and the nucleusLO 1

Prototypical eukaryotic cell

  • The cell is organized into nucleus + cytoplasm; the fluid part of the cytoplasm is the cytosol.
  • Cytosol is about pH 7.2, mildly more acidic than extracellular fluid at about pH 7.4.
  • In this handout, the nucleus and nucleolus are the organelles emphasized as visible by light microscopy; most other organelles require electron microscopy.
  • Membrane-bound organelles create controlled microenvironments that can differ markedly from the cytosol.
  • A relatively increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio is associated with malignant cells.

Chromatin

  • Nucleosome: DNA wrapped around an octamer of histones, two each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4.
  • Heterochromatin: condensed and transcriptionally silent; associated with DNA methylation and histone deacetylation.
  • Euchromatin: less condensed and transcriptionally active; histone acetylation and DNA demethylation favor accessibility.
  • Nucleolus: rRNA transcription, pre-rRNA processing, and ribosomal-subunit assembly.
  • Nuclear pores: regulated import/export routes for RNA, ribosomal subunits, transcription factors, and other proteins.
Memory hook
Euchromatin = accessible/expression. Heterochromatin = highly condensed. The nucleolus is the ribosome-production center.
Current handout page 4. Nuclear ultrastructure, chromatin states, nucleolus, and nuclear-pore transport are all explicitly developed in the current handout.
02Organelle function and clinical discriminatorsLO 1
StructureCore function in this deckHigh-yield discriminator
MitochondriaAerobic ATP generation; Krebs cycle, electron transport, oxidative phosphorylation; additional metabolic pathways.Double membrane; matrix about pH 8.0; own circular DNA and ribosomes; high-energy tissues are most vulnerable to dysfunction.
Rough ERProduction and processing of membrane-embedded and secreted proteins.Ribosome-studded surface; ER lumen is oxidizing, Ca2+-rich, and topologically equivalent to extracellular space.

PeroxisomeVery-long-chain fatty-acid beta-oxidation, branched-chain fatty-acid alpha-oxidation, free-radical handling.Catalase converts H2O2 to H2O. Deck links defects to X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and Zellweger syndrome.
RibosomeProtein synthesis.Prokaryotic 70S = 30S + 50S; eukaryotic 80S = 40S + 60S.
ProteasomeQuality control and degradation of endogenous cytosolic proteins.Polyubiquitination marks proteins; regulatory particles use ATP to unfold substrate; bortezomib inhibits proteasome function.
Centrosome/centrioleMicrotubule organization and spindle formation; centrioles can become basal bodies.Centriole = nine triplet microtubules. Primary cilium defects can cause ciliopathies such as polycystic kidney disease.
Current handout page 5. Mitochondrial structure and the current deck emphasis on high-energy tissues, matrix/cristae, and mitochondrial DNA.

Mitochondrial inheritance

  • Mitochondrial DNA is transmitted through the maternal line in the deck.
  • An affected male does not transmit a mitochondrial-DNA disorder to offspring.
  • Heteroplasmy explains variable mutation load and variable severity between tissues and among children.
  • Nuclear-gene defects that impair mitochondrial proteins can produce similar organ dysfunction but do not follow maternal mitochondrial inheritance.
Current handout page 9. Lysosome and peroxisome are intentionally contrasted in the handout by pH, enzymes, metabolic role, and associated disease examples.
Do not miss
The current handout explicitly states that circulating fully differentiated red blood cells retain proteasomes but no other organelles. That is a favorite one-line discriminator because it combines cell structure with RBC physiology.
03Plasma membrane and lipid asymmetryLO 2

Leaflet composition

  • Inner/cytosolic leaflet: higher phosphatidylserine (PS), phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), and phosphatidylinositol (PI).
  • Outer leaflet: higher phosphatidylcholine (PC), sphingomyelin (SM), and glycolipids.
  • Carbohydrates are also predominantly displayed on the outer surface.
TranslocaseDirection/function in current deckATP?
FlippaseMoves selected phospholipids toward the inner/cytosolic monolayer and helps create/maintain asymmetry.Energy-dependent
FloppaseMoves polar lipids toward the outer/extracellular or luminal monolayer; deck identifies these as ABC-family transporters.Energy-dependent
ScramblaseBidirectional lipid exchange that dissipates asymmetry.No ATP in the deck
Why asymmetry matters
PS exposure on the outer surface can mark apoptotic cells for phagocytic clearance. In platelets/erythrocytes, calcium-dependent scrambling can also generate a procoagulant surface.
Current handout page 15. The current deck directly maps inner versus outer leaflet lipids and links phosphatidylserine externalization to scramblase activation and apoptosis.
04Membrane permeability and transport mechanismsLO 3

What crosses a naked lipid bilayer?

Gases and lipophilic molecules cross most readily. Hydrophilic nutrients, waste products, and ions require membrane proteins to cross efficiently.

MechanismProtein?Energy?DirectionKey behavior
Simple diffusionNo transport protein requiredNoDown concentration gradientNot carrier-limited
Facilitated diffusionChannel or carrierNoDown concentration gradientSpecific; carrier-mediated transport can saturate and can show competitive inhibition
Primary active transportPump/transporterDirect ATPCan move solute against gradientNa+/K+-ATPase is the central example
Secondary active transportCotransporterUses stored electrochemical-gradient energyOne solute can move against its gradientSymport = same direction; antiport = opposite directions

Channel versus carrier

  • Channels form pores and allow very rapid ion movement down an electrochemical gradient. The deck distinguishes voltage-gated, ligand-gated, and mechanically gated channels.
  • Carriers/transporters bind a solute and change conformation. Their finite number produces saturation.
  • The deck uses CFTR as an ATP-gated anion-channel example and a sodium-dependent glucose cotransporter as a secondary-active symporter example.
Current handout page 18. The handout separates facilitated diffusion from active transport and emphasizes specificity, saturation, competitive inhibition, and energy use.
05Na+/K+-ATPase and ion-gradient functionsLO 4
Pump stoichiometry
1 ATP -> 3 Na+ out + 2 K+ in. The pump is electrogenic because more positive charge leaves than enters.

Three gradients generated

  1. Outside-to-inside Na+ gradient
  2. Inside-to-outside K+ gradient
  3. Inside-negative electrical potential

In polarized cells, the deck places the pump on the basolateral membrane.

Primary versus secondary active transport

Primary active transport spends ATP directly. Secondary active transport uses energy already stored in an ion gradient. A symporter carries coupled solutes in the same direction; an antiporter carries them in opposite directions.

Current handout page 22. Current handout page 22 shows the six-step Na+/K+-ATPase cycle, its 3:2 stoichiometry, the three generated gradients, and secondary-active cotransport.

Cell communication

Na+ and K+ gradients permit neuronal depolarization and electrical signaling.

Muscle function

Ion gradients support skeletal and cardiac muscle excitability and contraction.

Enzyme regulation

The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger helps keep cytosolic Ca2+ low until signaling raises it.

Hormone secretion

The deck explicitly links ionic gradients and Ca2+ signaling to secretion, including insulin release from pancreatic beta cells.

Current handout page 24. The deck summarizes biological uses of electrochemical gradients: communication, muscle function, enzyme regulation, and hormone secretion.
06Quiz-ready concept mapAll LOs

Discriminations worth testing

  • Euchromatin vs heterochromatin: accessibility, transcription, acetylation/methylation direction.
  • RER vs SER vs Golgi: protein production, lipid/detox/Ca2+, modification/sorting.
  • Lysosome vs peroxisome vs proteasome: acid hydrolases, VLCFA/H2O2 metabolism, ubiquitin-tagged endogenous protein degradation.
  • Mitochondrial DNA vs nuclear-encoded mitochondrial disease: maternal inheritance only applies to mtDNA defects.
  • Flippase/floppase vs scramblase: maintained asymmetry versus bidirectional scrambling.
  • Channel vs carrier: pore/speed/gating versus binding/conformational change/saturation.
  • Facilitated diffusion vs active transport: both can require proteins, but only active transport uses energy to drive uphill movement.
  • Primary vs secondary active transport: direct ATP versus gradient energy.
  • Symport vs antiport: same direction versus opposite directions.
  • Na+/K+-ATPase consequence: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in -> Na+ gradient, K+ gradient, inside-negative potential -> downstream cellular work.
